prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube in first place, and I still think opening the high-energy neutrino sky is the kind of clue from nature that I value. But reading the ballots, I move the topological insulator discovery to the top of my preferred configuration. It is the one candidate that most of the committee ranks highly (seven of eight rank it, five place it in their top three), and the reason is scientific rather than a matter of politeness. Kane and Mele made a sharp theoretical proposal, a Z2 invariant that fixes protected edge states, and Molenkamp's group then went into the laboratory and saw the quantum spin Hall edge channels in HgTe in 2007. That is theory being confronted with nature and surviving, over fifteen years and many independent platforms (transport, ARPES, STM, first-principles materials prediction). The concept has spread far beyond solids. It is mature, stable and, as several colleagues say, arguably overdue. A Kane, Mele, Molenkamp prize gives a discovery-first citation with a theory pair and the decisive experiment.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted that HgTe wells would be the right system, and the Molenkamp experiment was a test of that prediction; they are outside the credited names, as are Fu, Moore and Balents for the 3D generalisation. Hasan's ARPES observation of the 3D topological insulator is a separate strand that a three-person prize leaves out. Topological phases were also recognised in 2016 (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz), so a sceptic may call this a second helping of the same theme, and practical impact is still modest. If the committee judges that the omissions make a fair three-name configuration impossible, I would fall back on a cleaner discovery with a short, clear list of names.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first with me, values the detector-driven discovery and sees a single-laureate Halzen prize as clean, while admitting that the collaboration scale makes the single name hard to judge.
responses.response: I share the enthusiasm and I will not pretend I have dropped IceCube; it stays as my first alternative. But your own reservation and mine point the same way: a one-person prize for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds, built on AMANDA and DUMAND, invites a credit dispute that the committee cannot easily settle from this list, and only the two of us put it first. I would rather bring it back if our colleagues find that the condensed-matter options cannot be allocated fairly. You also place the topological insulators fourth and say you defer on attribution; I would ask you to judge the discovery by its confirmation record, which is exceptionally strong.

responses.point: Eriksson proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for topological insulators, noting that the package has more than three strong claimants and that the 2016 prize is context but not an obstacle.
responses.response: I agree about the 2016 prize and about the crowded claimant list, but I part from you on Hasan over Mele. The prize is for a discovery, and the discovery that has a clean before and after is the quantum spin Hall effect: the Kane-Mele proposal and the HgTe observation. Hasan's 3D ARPES work is excellent but it is a follow-on that generalises the idea. Leaving out Mele, who shared the Z2 invariant and the model from the start, seems harder to defend than leaving out the 3D step. I would like to hear from you why you weigh ARPES above the original theory pair.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a simple, general and rigorous organising principle with a bulk invariant, but sees dropping Mele or choosing between Molenkamp and Hasan as a real allocation problem, and notes that BHZ are not credited.
responses.response: Your framing of the bulk invariant is exactly why I think the theory should be the core of the citation, and it is why I keep Mele. I would also say plainly that the BHZ proposal is the weakest point of this configuration. The HgTe experiment was designed from their prediction, and a citation that names only Kane and Mele on the theory side tells a slightly incomplete story. I do not see a way to resolve that within three names, so I would treat it as an open uncertainty rather than hide it, and word the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect itself.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp second and puts weight on the experimental confirmation, noting the 2016 prize did not cover this discovery and that the graphene spin-orbit gap was too small for the original Kane-Mele proposal to be realised.
responses.response: The last point matters more than it first seems. The original graphene realisation failed because the gap is tiny, and the effect was first seen in HgTe following a different theoretical proposal. This is exactly why the experimental share has to carry weight in the citation, and why I cannot accept a theory-only prize. I agree with you that a four-way split with Hasan is unattractive, and I read the experimental confirmation as the decisive element.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as a simple physical trick (magic wavelength) opening a new precision regime, a clean two-person credit, and a natural continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb prize.
responses.response: I find the clock case serious and I ranked it below the cut only because it was not among my own top choices; the two-name credit is the cleanest on the table, and the maturity is not in doubt. Where I hesitate is that Ye's work sits on the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes already given, so the committee has to decide whether a lattice clock is a new discovery or a refinement of precision measurement. I am not convinced it is a refinement, but I would like a sharper statement of what in nature or in measurement the lattice clock showed that was not already shown. If that can be made, I could place it first in a configuration.

uncertainties: Whether a three-name configuration of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can be defended given the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and Hasan's 3D work, or whether the committee prefers Hasan over Mele.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases will make a second topology prize look repetitive.
Whether a single-name IceCube prize for Halzen can be justified at all, given the AMANDA and DUMAND lineage and the collaboration scale.
Whether optical lattice clocks count as a distinct discovery or a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot, and none of the credited people is at Uppsala as far as the provided profile shows.
